world.setting: 19th-century America: from Baltimore shipyards and Chesapeake Bay slave farms to the abolitionist lecture halls of Rochester, the Civil War White House, and Washington D.C. during Reconstruction
world.register: documentary historical biography — rigorous archival narrative, soaring prophetic rhetoric, political drama

douglass.name: Frederick Douglass
douglass.role: escaped slave, towering orator, abolitionist leader, and statesman
douglass.look: A tall, commanding African American man in his 40s with intense dark eyes, thick halo of swept-back gray-streaked hair, sharp jawline, and solemn dignified expression, wearing a tailored 19th-century black wool frock coat, crisp white wing-collar shirt, and silk cravat.

lincoln.name: Abraham Lincoln
lincoln.look: A gaunt, weathered 55-year-old man with deep facial creases, melancholy gray eyes, dark untidy hair, and a chiseled chin-curtain beard, wearing an unbuttoned black broadcloth frock coat, rumpled white linen shirt, black bow tie, and holding a tall silk stovepipe hat.

brown.name: John Brown
brown.look: A fierce, sun-leathered 59-year-old man with intense piercing blue eyes, high forehead, and a massive untamed white-gray beard flowing down his chest, wearing a coarse wool frontier coat and heavy boots.

garrison.name: William Lloyd Garrison
garrison.role: pacifist abolitionist editor of The Liberator
garrison.look: A clean-shaven, bespectacled 45-year-old intellectual with a balding dome, wire-rimmed spectacles perched on a sharp nose, and pursed puritanical lips, wearing a severe black high-collared Quaker suit and pristine white stock.

covey.name: Edward Covey
covey.look: A wiry, sun-hardened 35-year-old man with a squinting predatory gaze, thin cruel mouth, and rough sandy-brown stubble, wearing a dusty sweat-stained homespun linen work shirt, broad leather suspenders, and mud-encrusted trousers.

sophia-auld.name: Sophia Auld
sophia-auld.role: Baltimore slave mistress who taught young Douglass the alphabet
sophia-auld.look: A 30-year-old woman with a compassionate but conflicted countenance, dark brown hair gathered in neat side-braids beneath a simple white lace cap, wearing a mid-19th-century calico day dress and linen apron.

hugh-auld.name: Hugh Auld
hugh-auld.look: A burly, authoritative 40-year-old man with heavy muttonchop sideburns, furrowed brow, and gruff expression, wearing an iron-gray wool waistcoat over a work shirt and dark wool trousers.

narrator.name: David W. Blight
narrator.role: Pulitzer Prize-winning biographer and Yale historian
narrator.look: A thoughtful 65-year-old historian with short silver-gray hair, kind observant eyes behind horn-rimmed glasses, wearing a tailored brown tweed blazer over an ivory oxford shirt in an archival library.

everyman.name: Enslaved Worker / Union Soldier
everyman.role: 19th-century enslaved laborer and Civil War freedom fighter
everyman.look: A resilient 19th-century African American laborer in ragged coarse osnaburg cotton tunic, weathered trousers, and worn leather work boots standing against an antebellum landscape.

baltimoreShipyards.look: 19th-century Baltimore Fell's Point waterfront docks with wooden sailing frigates, oak timber piles, pitch barrels, caulking irons, and brick warehouses beneath overcast maritime skies.

coveyFarm.look: A windswept, desolate Chesapeake Bay farmstead in Talbot County with weathered timber barns, muddy animal pens, split-rail fences, and winter woods.

corinthianHall.look: Neoclassical Corinthian Hall in Rochester with polished oak lectern, crimson velvet curtains, brass gaslight chandeliers, and tiered wooden galleries.

whiteHouseOffice.look: Abraham Lincoln's Executive Mansion office during wartime with high ceilings, tall draped windows, tall mahogany bookcases, military maps of Virginia pinned to walls, and candle-wax encrusted desk.

chambersburgQuarry.look: An overgrown abandoned stone quarry in Chambersburg, Pennsylvania with damp limestone ledges, deep shadows, and tangled pines at twilight.

cedarHillEstate.look: Douglass's Cedar Hill mansion parlor in Anacostia with tall Victorian bookshelves, walnut rolltop desk, velvet armchairs, framed portraits, and panoramic view of Washington D.C.

capitolPortico.look: The muddy east front of the U.S. Capitol on March 4, 1865, under rainy skies, with wooden inaugural scaffolding, massive newly-crowned iron dome, and sprawling crowds in damp broadcloth.

auldKitchen.look: A warm Baltimore townhome brick kitchen with cast iron hearth, pine work table, baking flour, and alphabet primers hidden among ledger books.

objects.why: The American Civil War and the moral struggle against chattel slavery.
Physical shackles of plantation bondage and the fugitive slave status.
The Columbian Orator and Douglass's life-saving acquisition of literacy.
The US Constitution, the Fugitive Slave Act, Dred Scott decision, and Emancipation Proclamation.
Armed resistance, John Brown's broadswords, and the combat arms of the 54th Massachusetts.
The heavy human toll of slavery and hundreds of thousands of Civil War war dead.
Apocalyptic retributive justice, burning cities, and prophetic wrath.
Constitutional protection and military defense of emancipated citizens.
The North Star abolitionist newspaper, letters, and speeches.
Justice, moral accountability, and the weighing of American founding promises.
Cedar Hill estate in Anacostia and the longing for domestic sanctuary.
The Underground Railroad and the arduous path from slavery to northern freedom.

spine.claim: Douglass discovers that literacy and physical self-defense are revolutionary acts that liberate the mind before the law liberates the body.
Douglass breaks with Garrisonian purist pacifism to deploy constitutional politics and the abolitionist press against slavery.
Douglass supports armed resistance but avoids John Brown's doomed raid, transforming the Civil War into an apocalyptic crusade for Black freedom.
Douglass directly confronts Lincoln to secure rights for Black soldiers, celebrating emancipation as the vindication of his prophetic warnings.
From Cedar Hill, Douglass watches the bitter betrayal of Reconstruction, concluding that freedom in America is a perpetual struggle rather than a permanent triumph.
